title: Canada Reverses Work Permit Restriction After Policy Was Posted in Error
excerpt: IRCC corrected instructions that would have barred workers not currently employed abroad from obtaining reciprocal employment work permits, calling it a version control mistake.
body:
• Canada's immigration department has reversed a rule change that would have limited reciprocal employment work permits to workers already employed outside Canada.
  • IRCC said the restrictive language "was posted in error due to a version control issue" and corrected it on August 6, 2026.
  • Reciprocal employment work permits (code C20) are LMIA-exempt, making them faster and easier to obtain than permits through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program.
  • The permits are commonly used by multinational corporations, international non-profits, and governmental organizations.

Canada's immigration department has walked back a policy change that would have significantly restricted who can obtain reciprocal employment work permits — a key pathway used by multinational companies to transfer workers to Canada without a Labour Market Impact Assessment.

What Happened

On July 29, 2026, Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) published updated instructions to officers specifying that applicants for reciprocal employment work permits "must be currently employed by the company abroad" and could not receive a permit if their employment was set to begin only upon arrival in Canada, according to CIC News.

The restriction would have been a major change to the International Mobility Program (IMP) work permits issued under code C20, potentially blocking thousands of workers who had accepted offers from multinational employers but had not yet started working abroad.

IRCC has now confirmed the restrictive language was never intended policy. According to a statement by an immigration department official, circulated in an email to immigration lawyers and reviewed by CIC News, the change "was posted in error due to a version control issue and does not reflect the intended policy."

The Corrected Policy

On August 6, IRCC published a corrected version of the instructions, removing the section that required current foreign employment. The original eligibility criteria for C20 work permits remain intact.

Reciprocal employment work permits under the IMP are exempt from the Labour Market Impact Assessment (LMIA) requirement, making them considerably faster and less expensive to obtain than permits through the Temporary Foreign Worker Program (TFWP). They are issued when hiring a foreign national in Canada creates or maintains similar employment opportunities abroad for Canadian citizens and permanent residents.

Who Uses These Permits

C20 work permits are most commonly used by multinational corporations, internationally operating non-profits, and governmental organizations. They allow companies to bring employees to Canada as part of reciprocal staffing arrangements without proving that no Canadian worker is available for the role.

For Indian workers, these permits are particularly relevant at global consulting firms, technology companies, and financial institutions that routinely transfer staff between offices in India, the United States, and Canada.

Why It Matters for Indian Workers in Canada

The episode is a reminder of how quickly immigration policy can shift — and how version control errors in government publishing can create real confusion for applicants and employers. Had the restriction stood, it would have narrowed an important entry pathway at a time when Canada is already tightening temporary immigration across multiple categories.

Indian nationals represent the largest group of work permit holders in Canada. Any changes to IMP eligibility criteria directly affect this community's mobility between global offices.

What's Next

Immigration lawyers who flagged the error have confirmed the corrected instructions are now live on the IRCC website. Workers and employers who may have delayed applications based on the July 29 instructions can proceed under the original rules. However, the incident highlights the importance of monitoring IRCC updates closely, as even inadvertent changes can disrupt pending applications.
